sections.figure_alt: A real-axis segment joining two pole marks.
sections.body_md:
The root locus draws the closed-loop poles as one gain \(K\) runs from zero to infinity. Each branch starts at an open-loop pole, because that is where the closed-loop poles sit when \(K = 0\). It ends at an open-loop zero, or it runs to infinity when there are more poles than zeros.

You sketch it from a few rules instead of solving the characteristic equation at every gain. The real-axis rule, the asymptotes, the breakaway points, and the departure angles are enough to see whether a branch is heading into the right half-plane.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Positive gain means \(1 + KG(s) = 0\). A real test point is on that locus when an odd number of real poles and zeros lie to its right. With \(n\) poles and \(m\) zeros the asymptote angles are
\[
\frac{(2q+1)\,180^\circ}{n-m},
\]
and they meet at the centroid \((\sum p - \sum z)/(n-m)\). A breakaway on the real axis is a repeated root, where \(dK/ds = 0\). The departure angle from a pole is \(180^\circ\) minus the angles of the vectors from the other poles, plus the angles of the vectors from the zeros.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take poles at \(-1.5\) and \(-8.5\), and no zeros. They meet on the real axis at the midpoint \(-5\). The gain on \(1/((s+1.5)(s+8.5))\) is \(K = -(s+1.5)(s+8.5)\). At \(s = -5\) that product of distances is \(3.5 \cdot 3.5\), so \(K = 17.5\). Past that gain the two branches leave the real axis as a complex pair. The centroid of the asymptotes is the same point, \(-5\), and the positive-gain asymptotes are the vertical lines through it.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The angles \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) for a two-pole excess are the negative-gain locus. Positive gain uses the odd multiples, \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\). The real-axis count includes zeros, not only poles, and it counts marks to the right, not to the left. A departure angle forgets a zero's contribution if you only subtract pole angles. And the locus shows poles against gain. It does not replace a Nyquist plot, which sweeps frequency at a fixed gain.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Seeing where a branch crosses the imaginary axis tells you the gain a loop shape cannot exceed. Lead and lag then move that picture by adding their own poles and zeros. The same crossing is one way to meet the bandwidth limits that right-half-plane zeros and delays impose, and a disk of plant uncertainty is stable only when every nearby locus stays in the left half-plane.
